newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda plans to produce instant coffee by end-1997.
newsitem.headline: Uganda plans to produce instant coffee by end-1997.

text.p: Uganda and a Spanish consortium led by coffee exporter Eurocafe have entered a joint venture to build a factory to produce instant coffee by the end of 1997, Ugandan coffee authorities said on Tuesday.
William Okecho, coordinator of the privatisation of the Coffee Marketing Board, told Reuters the new project was valued at $9 million, of which $4 million would be share capital.
The Ugandan government has contributed land for the factory and share capital of around $2 million. That will entitle it to 49 percent shareholding in the factory.

The consortium led by Eurocafe will inject into the project $2 million as venture capital and will also provide another $5 million in machinery and construction materials. That will give the consortium a 51 percent shareholding in the factory.
"The total project will be turnkey, and will cost $9 million," Okecho told Reuters. "We expect it to be operational in 12 months from now."

Okecho said production of instant Ugandan coffee was seen by the government as a measure to add value to its product. The new factory would have an initial capacity of 2,000 tonnes of instant coffee that would require 5,000 tonnes of green coffee.

That will be a very small percentage of Uganda's annual production. Last year, Uganda exported around 4.1 million 60-kg bags of coffee. Some 88 percent of its produce is robusta while 12 percent is arabica.
Okecho said Uganda had been successful in selling coffee to Spain. "The Spanish market is more or less captured and we hope that will spread (across Europe)," he told Reuters.
The instant coffee will be given a brand name, Okecho said.
Okecho said the new company would not have a monopoly in the instant coffee business in Uganda and that after the project took off the government would sell its shares to the public.

"We are not about to create monopolies here. We intend to divest our 49 percent shareholding to Ugandans," he said. He hinted that might be through a Kampala Stock Exchange, which would be operational long before the factory's operational date.
